meta.name: Hyperproof
meta.title: Hyperproof ad teardown: a precise privacy hook, a generic compliance page
meta.meta_desc: A teardown of Hyperproof's live LinkedIn ad: one of the sharpest hooks in the series, built for a DPO, lands on a broad GRC page where the words that made the ad work disappear.
meta.og_desc: Built for a DPO. The page was built for everyone.

hook: The ad spoke to one person.
voice.lede: The ad is built for one very specific person, a DPO or privacy lead responsible for sub-processors, personal data and GDPR exposure, and its hook is one of the sharpest in the series. Then the landing page switches to a broad GRC story for CISOs, compliance and internal audit. The words that made the ad work, sub-processor, personal data, disappear. The ad has focus, the page has assets, the funnel just needs alignment.

findings.title: A hook built for exactly one buyer
findings.what: “You approved the vendor. Who approved their sub-processors?” is clear in under 12 words and gives a privacy team a concrete reason to click. It speaks to one buyer, the privacy lead, and does not try to speak to anyone else.

findings.title: The page itself is not weak
findings.what: Strong structure, credible customer logos (Reddit, Nutanix, Fortinet, Appian), a genuinely low-friction four-field form, no credit card and no vendor logins. As a page, it has real assets.

findings.title: The words that earned the click disappear
findings.what: The page switches to a broad TPRM and GRC story for CISOs and audit. “Sub-processor” and “personal data,” the exact words that made the privacy lead click, are gone. A precise privacy click lands on a generic compliance page.
findings.fix: Build a privacy-lead version of the page, or at least a section above the fold that keeps the sub-processor and personal-data language the ad used, so the buyer sees their own problem continue.

faq.a: Yes, the hook is one of the sharpest in the series: under 12 words, aimed at exactly one buyer, the DPO or privacy lead, with a concrete reason to click. It scores 6 overall because the funnel loses that focus after the click, not because the ad is weak.

On the landing page. The ad speaks to a privacy lead about sub-processors and personal data; the page switches to a broad GRC and TPRM story for CISOs, compliance and audit, and the specific privacy language disappears. The page has good assets, just aimed at a different buyer.

Keep the buyer the ad chose. Carry the sub-processor and personal-data language onto the page, at least above the fold, so the privacy lead sees their own problem continue instead of landing on a generic compliance pitch.

faq.q: How do I check my own ad for this?
faq.a: Find the two or three words in your ad that make your buyer click, then check the page: are those words still there above the fold? If a tightly-targeted ad lands on a broad page, the focus that earned the click leaks away. AdRoast scores this automatically, and the first roast is free.
